title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A present-tense verb ends in a letter that names its subject, so the pronoun stays out: hablo (I speak) · hablas (you speak) · habla (he or she speaks). The -o for "I" is the same in all three families — hablo, como, vivo.
The infinitive's ending sets the family, and the family decides the vowel in the other endings: hablar → hablas, hablamos; comer → comes; vivir → vives. -ar takes an a, -er and -ir take an e.

A daily-routine verb often carries a little pronoun that belongs to the verb and changes with the person: me levanto (I get up) · te levantas (you get up) · se levanta (he or she gets up). English has no word there at all, so the me is the piece that goes missing.

The a in front of a person is not "to". When the direct object of a verb is a specific person, Spanish puts a in front of them and English translates it as nothing at all: Veo a mi hermana is "I see my sister". A thing never takes it — Veo la casa.
The same little a marks a time: a las ocho is "at eight". One word, pointing at whatever comes next — a time, a specific person, and from M6 a destination.
Clock time is feminine and plural: las ocho is literally "the eight (hours)", so the article is there every time — a las ocho, never a ocho.
A part of the day is a whole phrase built on por: por la mañana · por la tarde · por la noche. Three words, one meaning, and the la is not optional.
todos los días — literally "all the days" — is how Spanish says "every day". It travels as one block and can open the sentence or close it.
An accent can be the whole word: cómo asks "how" (M2) and como means "I eat". Same five letters, and only the mark tells them apart — as it does for qué, which asks, beside que, which joins.
A question word goes to the front and takes its little preposition with it: ¿A qué hora te levantas? English is happy to leave it dangling — "What time do you get up at?" — and Spanish never is.

words.note: hablar, to speak — the model -ar verb. The -o ending is the "I", so no pronoun is needed: hablo (I) · hablas (you) · habla (he, she and usted).
Literally "all the days" — three words for "every day", and the los cannot be dropped. The block moves as one thing, to the front of the sentence or to the end.

sentences.trap: English needs both words — I speak. Spanish packs the "I" into the ending, and putting yo back in front makes the sentence emphatic rather than neutral.
sentences.sound: A-blo. The h is silent, as it is in hola, and the stress is on the first syllable.

variations.changed: drop the time block — the sentence is still complete
the block moves to the front and nothing else changes

mistake.why: The los is part of the phrase: todos los días.

sentences.mnemonic: -o is the "I" in every family: hablo, como, vivo.

words.note: levantarse, "to raise oneself". The little pronoun is part of the verb and changes with the person: me levanto (I get up) · te levantas (you get up) · se levanta (he or she gets up).

A one-letter signpost pointing at whatever comes next. In front of a clock time it is "at": a las ocho. In front of a specific person it marks that person as the object and is translated as nothing: Veo a mi hermana. From M6 it also points at a destination — voy a México, fui a India.
Eight o'clock. Spanish counts the hours as feminine plurals — "the eights" — so the las never disappears: a las ocho. M8 teaches the numbers on their own.

sentences.trap: "I get up" has nothing in it that answers to me, so the me is the piece an English speaker drops. Levanto a las ocho is not a sentence.
sentences.sound: le-VAN-to. The v is soft — a Spanish v sits somewhere between an English b and v.

variations.changed: the pronoun and the ending move together: me/-o → te/-as
a plain time word instead of a clock time, and then no a

mistake.why: The verb needs its pronoun: Me levanto a las ocho.

sentences.usage: The first line of any description of your day.

sentences.cue: In the morning I eat bread

words.note: "In the morning", and all three words are fixed: por, then la, then mañana. Its partners — por la tarde, por la noche — are separate phrases of the same shape rather than other forms of this one. Much of Latin America also says en la mañana; por la mañana is understood everywhere. On its own, mañana means "tomorrow", which M6 teaches.
comer, to eat, in the "I" form: como (I) · comes (you) · come (he or she). Without an accent it is not M2's cómo — cómo asks "how", como eats, and the mark is the only difference.

sentences.trap: English says "in the morning". Spanish says por la mañana, with por where you expect "in" and with a la that English throws away.
sentences.sound: ma-ÑA-na. The ñ is the ny of "canyon" — the double n of an English "manana" is not it.

variations.cue: In the afternoon I eat bread
variations.changed: the same frame, a different part of the day

variations.cue: I eat bread in the morning
variations.changed: the time phrase moves to the end

mistake.why: cómo with an accent is the question word "how". The verb is como.

sentences.usage: Describing the shape of your day.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent asks; the bare word eats.

words.note: "At night", built exactly like por la mañana and a separate phrase from it. Spanish's noche starts earlier than English's "night": dinner at nine is por la noche.
estudiar in the "I" form. That is three shapes of one verb now: un estudiante is the person, estudiar is the plain verb, estudio is what I do.

sentences.trap: Spanish has no separate word for the evening: la noche covers what English splits into evening and night, and la tarde runs until it gets dark.
sentences.sound: NO-che, with the ch of "church" — never a k.

variations.changed: drop the object; the verb carries the sentence on its own

variations.cue: I study Spanish in the morning
variations.changed: the same habit in a different slot of the day

mistake.why: The la is part of the phrase: por la noche.

sentences.usage: Pairing a habit with a time of day.
sentences.mnemonic: por la + the part of the day, every time.

words.note: vivir, to live — the -ir family. Its endings sit very close to the -er family's: vivo (I) · vives (you) · vive (he or she).
"My". It ignores the gender of what is owned — mi hermana, mi libro — and goes plural only with the thing: mis libros. The owner never shows on it.
Sister, feminine: la hermana. Its masculine partner hermano is a different word — brother — and not another ending of this one; the plural hermanos covers a mixed set, "brothers and sisters".

sentences.trap: mis is the one place English's "my" would have to change: the ending follows the number of the thing owned, never the owner.
sentences.sound: VI-vo, and both v's are soft — closer to a b than to an English v.

variations.changed: a different person, not a different ending of the same word

variations.cue: I don't live with my sister
variations.changed: the no goes in front of the verb, exactly as in M3

mistake.why: mis goes with a plural thing: mi hermana, mis hermanas.

sentences.mnemonic: mi for one thing, mis for more — the owner never shows.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-see [a] my sister" — the a marks a person and is not translated

words.note: ver, to see: veo (I) · ves (you) · ve (he or she). The "I" form keeps the e of the stem — veo, not vo.

sentences.trap: The a is not "to". Veo a mi hermana is plain "I see my sister", and leaving the a out is the mistake — not the tidier version.
sentences.sound: VE-o, two syllables, and both vowels are sounded.

variations.changed: any specific person takes the a
a thing takes no a at all

mistake.why: A specific person in the object seat takes a: Veo a mi hermana.

sentences.usage: Talking about the people in your day.
sentences.mnemonic: A person in the object seat wears an a.

sentences.cue: What time do you get up?

words.note: "What", with the accent, because it is asking. Unaccented que is the joining word "that" — the mark is the whole difference, exactly as it is between cómo and como.
Hour, and "time" when the clock is what you are asking about: ¿A qué hora? is "at what time". Feminine: la hora.

sentences.trap: English can leave the preposition dangling at the end — "What time do you get up at?". Spanish sends the a to the front with the question word and never leaves it behind.
sentences.sound: The h of hora is silent, so the words run together: a-qué-O-ra.

variations.cue: What time do you get up, Ana?
variations.changed: add the name after a comma
the answer, with the a and the hour back in place

mistake.why: The a is part of the question: ¿A qué hora te levantas? Without it you have asked what the time is.

sentences.mnemonic: The a goes to the front with the question: ¿A qué hora…?

words.note: trabajar, to work: trabajo (I) · trabajas (you) · trabaja (he or she). The same word is also the noun "work" or "a job" — el trabajo — and only the sentence around it decides which.
"In the afternoon", the third of the three: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche. La tarde runs from lunch until dark, which is why buenas tardes lasts so long.

sentences.trap: trabajo is both "I work" and "the job". Nothing inside the word chooses; an article in front of it does — el trabajo is the noun.
sentences.sound: tra-BA-jo. The j is a rasp from the back of the throat, like the ch of Scottish "loch".

variations.cue: I don't work in the afternoon

swap the time phrase for the block

sentences.mnemonic: Three parts of the day, one shape: por la ___.

words.note: trabajar for tú. The -as ending is the "you" of the -ar family; -er and -ir verbs use -es instead — comes, vives.

sentences.trap: There is still no "do" anywhere. The question is the statement with the marks around it, exactly as M2 showed.
sentences.sound: tra-BA-jas. The stress stays where it was when the ending changed.

variations.changed: swap the time phrase
the same words as a statement — only the marks and the tune change

mistake.why: The tú ending of an -ar verb is -as: trabajas. The -es belongs to comer and vivir.

sentences.display: Todos los días me levanto temprano
sentences.cue: Every day I get up early
sentences.glossEn: lit. "All the days myself I-raise early"
sentences.literal: All the days myself I-raise early

words.note: Early. Here it describes the getting-up rather than a person, so it has nothing to agree with and never changes shape. Its opposite is tarde, which is also the noun "afternoon".

sentences.trap: The -o on the end of temprano is not an agreement waiting to happen: an adverb has no gender to copy.
sentences.sound: tem-PRA-no. The r is a single tap, tucked inside the pr.

variations.changed: drop the block; the habit survives

variations.display: Todos los días me levanto a las ocho
variations.cue: Every day I get up at eight
variations.changed: a clock time instead of a plain one

mistake.display: Todos los días me levanto temprana
mistake.why: temprano is not describing a person here, so there is nothing for it to agree with: me levanto temprano.

sentences.usage: The line that ends most descriptions of a routine.
sentences.mnemonic: todos los días fits at either end of the sentence.
